info.text: Lesson 04 quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: What is a constant in C++?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A constant is like a variable with a lock: you must give it a value when you create it, and the compiler stops you from changing it afterwards.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: A named value that cannot change after it is initialized
A variable that can only store whole numbers
A comment that explains a number
A value that changes every time the program runs

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
const int MAX = 10;
cout << MAX * 2 << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Reading a constant is always allowed. MAX * 2 is 10 * 2 = 20. The constant itself stays 10.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
const int LIMIT = 5;
LIMIT = 6;
cout << LIMIT << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The second line tries to assign to a const. The compiler refuses, so there is no program to run at all: this is caught before the program ever starts.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which line correctly creates a constant?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The keyword is const (not constant), and a constant must receive its value on the very line where it is created, because it can never be assigned later.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: A shop uses the tax rate 0.15 in forty places in its code. What is the best way to make a future change easy?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A named constant gives the number a meaning and a single home. When the rate changes, you edit one line instead of hunting for forty.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Define const double TAX_RATE = 0.15; once and use the name everywhere
Type 0.15 everywhere and use find-and-replace when it changes
Store the rate in a char variable
Write a comment next to every 0.15

questiontext.text: What is the main difference between const and constexpr?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Both lock a value. constexpr goes further and demands that the value is known at compile time, which makes it usable in places that need a fixed size or fixed number.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: constexpr requires a value the compiler can compute while compiling; const only promises not to change
const is for numbers and constexpr is for text
constexpr values can be changed later, const values cannot
There is no difference at all

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines to calculate the seconds in a day. The program must print 86400.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Each constant is built from the one before it, so the chain must be written in order: 60, then 3600, then 86400.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
constexpr int SECONDS_PER_MINUTE = 60;
constexpr int SECONDS_PER_HOUR = SECONDS_PER_MINUTE * 60;
constexpr int SECONDS_PER_DAY = SECONDS_PER_HOUR * 24;
cout << SECONDS_PER_DAY << endl;

name.text: Q08 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct pieces into the gaps (the program prints 2 of 3).

main.cpp
[[1]] int MAX_LIVES = 3;
int lives = MAX_LIVES;
lives [[2]] 1;
cout << lives << " of " << MAX_LIVES << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. MAX_LIVES must never change, so it is a const. The variable lives goes down by one with -=. Note that == would only compare, not change.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
const int MAX_LIVES = 3;
int lives = MAX_LIVES;
lives -= 1;
cout << lives << " of " << MAX_LIVES << endl;

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#define SQUARE(x) x * x
cout << SQUARE(2 + 3) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A #define is plain text replacement. The preprocessor turns SQUARE(2 + 3) into 2 + 3 * 2 + 3, and multiplication happens first: 2 + 6 + 3 = 11. A real constant or function would give 25.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Why do many programmers avoid #define for constants?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The preprocessor knows nothing about types or scope, so mistakes are hard to find. A const or constexpr variable is checked by the compiler like every other variable.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: It is only text replacement: it has no type and no scope checking
It is not allowed in C++ at all

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
constexpr int A = 3;
constexpr int B = A * A;
cout << B + A << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A constant may be built from other constants. B is 3 * 3 = 9, and B + A is 9 + 3 = 12.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Match each literal with its type.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

42  →  [[1]]

42LL  →  [[2]]

3.14  →  [[3]]

3.14f  →  [[4]]

'x'  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The suffix LL makes an integer literal a long long, and the suffix f makes a decimal literal a float. Without a suffix, a decimal literal is a double.

The correct answer:

  • 42 → int
  • 42LL → long long
  • 3.14 → double
  • 3.14f → float
  • 'x' → char

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
float f = 0.1f;
double d = 0.1;
cout << (f == d) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A float keeps fewer digits than a double, so 0.1f and 0.1 are stored as slightly different numbers. They are not equal, and the comparison prints 0.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Sort each piece of code: does it compile or not?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

const int a = 1;  →  [[1]]

const int b;  →  [[2]]

constexpr int c = 2 + 3;  →  [[1]]

const int d = 4; d = 5;  →  [[2]]

constexpr int e = 10 / 2;  →  [[1]]

const int f = 3; int g = f * 2;  →  [[1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A constant must be initialized when it is created, and it can never be assigned afterwards. Using a constant in a calculation is always fine. Each line was tested with a real compiler.

The correct answer:

Compiles: const int a = 1;, constexpr int c = 2 + 3;, constexpr int e = 10 / 2;, const int f = 3; int g = f * 2;
Compile error: const int b;, const int d = 4; d = 5;

questiontext.text: What is a "magic number" in code?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Nobody can tell what 86400 means just by looking at it. Giving it a name like SECONDS_PER_DAY turns a mystery into documentation.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: An unexplained number typed directly into the code, such as 86400 or 0.15
A number that changes every time the program runs
A number created by a random generator

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
const int A = 6;
const int B = 4;
cout << A / B << " " << A % B << " " << static_cast<double>(A) / B << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Integer division gives 1 (6 / 4), the remainder is 2, and converting A to double first gives the exact result 1.5.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

name.text: Q17 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Choose the suffixes so the first literal is a long long and the second is a float.

Drag the correct pieces into the gaps.

main.cpp
long long big = 3000000000[[1]];
float ratio = 2.5[[2]];
cout << big << " " << ratio << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The suffix LL marks an integer literal as long long and f marks a decimal literal as float. The other pieces are not valid suffixes.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
long long big = 3000000000LL;
float ratio = 2.5f;
cout << big << " " << ratio << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each idea with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

const  →  [[1]]

constexpr  →  [[2]]

#define  →  [[3]]

Magic number  →  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These four ideas are the vocabulary of this lesson. Keep them straight and constants will feel easy.

The correct answer:

  • const → Promises that a value will not change
  • constexpr → The value must be computable while compiling
  • #define → Text replacement done by the preprocessor
  • Magic number → An unexplained number written directly in the code

questiontext.text:
Sort each property: does it describe a constant variable (const / constexpr) or a #define macro?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Has a real type such as int or double  →  [[1]]

Is plain text replaced before compiling  →  [[2]]

Follows normal scope rules  →  [[1]]

Can give surprising results like SQUARE(2 + 3)  →  [[2]]

Has no type at all  →  [[2]]

Shows up by name in a debugger  →  [[1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A constant variable is a real, typed, scoped citizen of the language. A macro is text pasted by the preprocessor, which is why it can behave in surprising ways.

The correct answer:

Constant variable: Has a real type such as int or double, Follows normal scope rules, Shows up by name in a debugger
#define macro: Is plain text replaced before compiling, Can give surprising results like SQUARE(2 + 3), Has no type at all

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so the program uses constants correctly. It must print 21.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]
 2  [[2]]
 3  [[3]]
 4  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. BASE must exist before SIZE uses it (SIZE = 20), and total uses SIZE (20 + 1 = 21). The print comes last.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
constexpr int BASE = 4;
constexpr int SIZE = BASE * 5;
int total = SIZE + 1;
cout << total << endl;
